history.title: History of Mountaineering
history.subtitle: From sacred heights to modern lightweight speed ascents
history.lead: Mountaineering began as exploration and science before transforming into one of the purest expressions of human endurance.

items.description: Pioneering ascents of the Wetterhorn and Matterhorn by Whymper, establishing the first Alpine standards.
Expeditions moved into the Caucasus, Andes, and the giants of the Karakoram and Himalaya.
Annapurna fell first in 1950, followed by Everest in 1953 by Hillary & Tenzing, and K2 in 1954.
Messner and Habeler proved summits could be reached without supplemental oxygen in self-contained teams.

types.title: Styles & Disciplines of Climbing
types.subtitle: How climbers approach the world's most formidable faces
types.lead: Each discipline demands distinct physical conditioning, technical systems, and psychological composure.

items.title: Alpine Style
items.description: Climbing with all gear and food in a continuous push without fixed ropes or supplementary oxygen.

items.title: Expedition / Siege Style
items.description: Establishing progressive high camps, fixed ropes, and rotating teams to haul supplies up 8,000m peaks.

items.title: Big Wall Climbing
items.description: Ascending sheer granite faces over multiple days, sleeping suspended on portable portaledges.

items.title: Mixed & Ice Climbing
items.description: Climbing frozen waterfalls and delicate interfaces of verglas, snow, and rock using modern ice tools.

items.title: Ski Mountaineering (Skimo)
items.description: Skinning up steep glaciated peaks with skis on pack, followed by a high-commitment descent.

techniques.title: Technical Progression in Sequence
techniques.subtitle: The structured order in which mountain craft is mastered
techniques.lead: Step by step, safety systems and movement discipline work together.

items.title: Movement & Precise Footwork
items.description: Centering gravity over footholds, trusting friction on granite, and kicking stable snow buckets.

items.title: Roping Up & Belaying
items.description: Tying certified figure-eight knots, constructing equalized multi-point anchors, and dynamic belaying.

items.title: Active & Passive Protection
items.description: Placing cams, hexes, nuts, and ice screws to ensure arresting capacity under severe fall forces.

items.title: Ice Axe Self-Arrest
items.description: Driving the adze and pick into snowpack within milliseconds of a slip to prevent momentum buildup.

items.title: Crevasse Rescue & Hauling
items.description: Rigging 3:1 Z-pulley or 5:1 complex hauling systems to extract fallen teammates from glacier crevasses.

items.title: Acclimatization & Pacing
items.description: Applying climb high, sleep low schedules to increase red blood cell count while monitoring SpO2.

sheltering.title: Sheltering Above the Treeline
sheltering.subtitle: Rest is a vital survival decision as terrain steepens
sheltering.lead: From comfortable European refuges to minimalist hanging portaledges in the Karakoram.

items.title: Mountain Huts & Refuges
items.description: Staffed alpine refuges providing hot broth, bunks, and route intelligence before alpine starts.

items.title: Base & High Altitude Camps
items.description: Geodesic expedition dome tents secured with deadman anchors to withstand 120 km/h storm winds.

items.title: Snow Caves & Quinzees
items.description: Hand-carved chambers into wind-drifted snow that trap body heat at 0°C during -40°C outside storms.

items.title: Bivouac Ledges (Bivy)
items.description: Minimalist emergency sacks on narrow rock ledges, clipped directly into anchor protection.

items.title: Suspended Portaledges
items.description: Engineered aluminum platform cots hanging from a single master point on overhanging big walls.

hazards.title: Mountain Hazards & Objective Risk
hazards.subtitle: Recognizing dangers early and having zero hesitation to turn back
hazards.lead: The mountain makes no compromises. Disciplined safety protocols preserve lives.

items.title: Avalanches & Slab Releases
items.description: Wind-loaded slabs on 30°–45° slopes. Mitigated with transceivers, probes, shovels, and snowpack pits.

items.title: Altitude Illness (AMS / HAPE / HACE)
items.description: Hypobaric hypoxia leading to fluid in lungs or brain. Prevented by pacing and immediate descent.

items.title: Concealed Glacial Crevasses
items.description: Chasms masked by fragile snow bridges. Traversed only on roped teams with rescue kits prepared.

items.title: Serac Collapse & Rockfall
items.description: Thermal expansion and shifting ice towers. Avoided by climbing in sub-zero early hours (2 AM starts).

items.title: Hypothermia & Frostbite
items.description: Severe wind chill. Prevented with 800-fill down suits, vapor barrier liners, and high-altitude boots.
